# Exercise 5.5 — Shrinking coefficients towards zero {#sec-regularisation}

**50 minutes · work individually**

::: {.callout-important}
## A suggested addition, not part of the original module
This exercise was proposed and drafted by the assistant that rebuilt the
booklet, not ported from an earlier version of the module. The word regularisation appears nowhere else in the booklet, although the site this material came from was called RegularizationAndTrees. Day 5 shows a forest beating a tree by averaging variance away; penalties are the other answer to the same problem. Treat it as a
draft to accept, rewrite or delete: nothing else depends on it, and removing it
means deleting this file and its line in `_quarto.yml`.
:::

:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell, run against
`data/diabetes.csv` with the split used throughout Day 5, plus four columns of
random numbers added on purpose.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Fit a lasso and a ridge logistic regression with the penalty chosen by
  cross-validation, in both languages, and read off which coefficients the
  penalty set to exactly zero.
- Say what each of the two penalties does to a predictor that carries no
  signal, and defend a choice between them to a reader.
- Show that the penalty which minimises cross-validated AUC is not the penalty
  that recovers the right variables, and quote the AUC the difference costs.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-random-forest answered the instability of a single tree by averaging:
grow five hundred trees on resampled rows and let the variance cancel. There is
a second answer to the same problem, and it does not need five hundred of
anything. Leave one model, and make it harder for the fitting procedure to give
any coefficient a large value. That is regularisation, and @sec-frameworks
already met it without arguing for it — scikit-learn applies a penalty by
default, R's `glmnet` engine applies one when asked, and the chapter closed by
saying that Day 5 would make the case. This is that case, and the case against.

It sits here, after @sec-resampling and @sec-decision-trees, because the
strength of the penalty is a hyperparameter like `tree_depth`: there is no way
to read it off the data you fitted on, and the only honest way to choose it is
the resampling machinery you already have.

## Worked example — twelve predictors, four of which are nothing

We take Day 5's eight predictors and add four columns of random numbers, drawn
independently of everything else and of each other. @sec-importance uses one
such control; four is better, because then the useless columns outnumber the
predictors that carry any real signal in this data — which, as Day 6 will show,
is roughly `glucose` and `age`.

Every predictor is standardised first. A penalty acts on the size of a
coefficient, and the size of a coefficient depends on the units of its
predictor, so penalising unstandardised predictors penalises whoever chose the
units. The standardisation happens inside the recipe or the pipeline, which is
what makes it honest under resampling (@sec-leakage).

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(tidymodels); library(readr)

dia <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(123)
dia <- dia |> mutate(noise  = round(rnorm(n()), 2),
                     noise2 = round(rnorm(n()), 2),
                     noise3 = round(rnorm(n()), 2),
                     noise4 = round(rnorm(n()), 2))
controls <- c("noise", "noise2", "noise3", "noise4")

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

norm_rec <- recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

plain_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(norm_rec) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm")) |>
  fit(data = train)

tidy(plain_fit) |> arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) |> print(n = 13)
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

dia = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (dia["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X = dia.drop(columns="diabetes").copy()

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
for nm in ["noise", "noise2", "noise3", "noise4"]:
    X[nm] = rng.normal(size=len(X)).round(2)
controls = ["noise", "noise2", "noise3", "noise4"]

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=123, stratify=y)

def coefs(fitted):
    """The coefficients of a fitted pipeline, named, largest first."""
    s = pd.Series(fitted[-1].coef_[0], index=X.columns)
    return s.reindex(s.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)

plain = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(coefs(plain).round(3))
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two spellings of "no penalty", and one relevel that differs from the rest of Day 5
`LogisticRegression()` **always** penalises unless you stop it: the default
`C=1.0` is a ridge penalty, and `C=np.inf` is the unpenalised fit that matches
R's `glm` (@sec-frameworks). If you are on scikit-learn 1.7 or earlier, write
`penalty=None`, `penalty="l1"` and `penalty="l2"` where this page writes
`C=np.inf`, `l1_ratio=1` and `l1_ratio=0`; the older spellings still run on
1.8 and 1.9 but print a deprecation warning.

The factor levels here are `neg`, `pos` — the order @sec-importance uses, not
the `pos`, `neg` of @sec-classification-metrics. This page reads coefficients,
and with `neg` first the coefficients are for the probability of `pos`, so a
positive coefficient means higher risk. The price is `event_level = "second"`
in every yardstick call below.
:::

Now the test AUC, and the control columns' coefficients, from the same fit.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
augment(plain_fit, test) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

## Python

```{python}
round(roc_auc_score(y_te, plain.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]), 3)
```
:::

Read the two coefficient tables again, and find the controls. In R, `noise4`
has the fourth largest coefficient of the twelve, ahead of `pressure`, `age`,
`pedigree`, `insulin` and `triceps`, and its p-value is 0.043. In Python,
`noise3` is sixth of twelve, ahead of `age`. Nothing is wrong with either fit.
This is what maximum likelihood does when it is given twelve predictors and 537
patients: it spends a little of each coefficient on whatever the random columns
happen to line up with.

## Task 1 — Let a lasso choose the variables

Fit the same logistic regression with an L1 penalty, with the strength of the
penalty tuned by 10-fold cross-validation on the training rows. The test set
takes no part in the choice, for the reason @sec-decision-trees gave.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")

pen_grid <- tibble(penalty = 10^seq(-4, 0, length.out = 30))

lasso_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(norm_rec) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg(penalty = ______, mixture = ______) |> set_engine("glmnet"))

set.seed(123)
folds     <- vfold_cv(train, v = 10, strata = diabetes)
lasso_res <- tune_grid(lasso_wf, resamples = folds, grid = pen_grid,
                       metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
show_best(lasso_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 3)

best_pen  <- select_best(lasso_res, metric = "roc_auc")
lasso_fit <- finalize_workflow(lasso_wf, best_pen) |> fit(data = train)
lasso_co  <- tidy(lasso_fit) |> arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
print(lasso_co, n = 13)

check_selection(lasso_co, controls, label = "the CV-best lasso")
check_metric_range(
  augment(lasso_fit, test) |>
    roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |> pull(.estimate),
  0.7, 0.95, "lasso test AUC")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the same placeholder you used for `tree_depth` in
@sec-decision-trees, so that the grid can supply the values. The second selects
which penalty you get: in `glmnet`'s parameterisation, `mixture` is the share
of the penalty that is L1, and the lasso is all of it.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")

pen_grid <- tibble(penalty = 10^seq(-4, 0, length.out = 30))

lasso_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(norm_rec) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet"))

set.seed(123)
folds     <- vfold_cv(train, v = 10, strata = diabetes)
lasso_res <- tune_grid(lasso_wf, resamples = folds, grid = pen_grid,
                       metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
show_best(lasso_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 3)

best_pen  <- select_best(lasso_res, metric = "roc_auc")
lasso_fit <- finalize_workflow(lasso_wf, best_pen) |> fit(data = train)
lasso_co  <- tidy(lasso_fit) |> arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
print(lasso_co, n = 13)

check_selection(lasso_co, controls, label = "the CV-best lasso")
check_metric_range(
  augment(lasso_fit, test) |>
    roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |> pull(.estimate),
  0.7, 0.95, "lasso test AUC")
```
:::

## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

Cs = np.logspace(-3, 2, 30)
cv = StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=123)

lasso_search = GridSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                  LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", l1_ratio=1,
                                     max_iter=5000)),
    {"logisticregression__C": Cs}, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc").fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(round(lasso_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"], 4),
      round(lasso_search.best_score_, 4))
lasso_co = coefs(lasso_search.best_estimator_)
print(lasso_co.round(4))

check_selection(lasso_co, controls, label="the CV-best lasso")
check_metric_range(roc_auc_score(y_te, lasso_search.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]),
                   0.7, 0.95, "lasso test AUC")
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## `penalty` and `C` run in opposite directions
R's `penalty` is the penalty itself: larger means more shrinkage. Python's `C`
is its reciprocal: larger means *less*. The two are related by
`C = 1 / (n * penalty)`, with `n = 537` training rows here, because `glmnet`
divides the likelihood by the sample size and scikit-learn does not. R's chosen
penalty of 0.0085 is therefore a `C` of 0.22, and Python's chosen `C` of 0.386
is a penalty of 0.0048. That is as close as two different splits of the same
768 patients were ever going to agree; the grids look unrelated and are not.
:::

The check prints `[fix]`, and the detail line says why. Write down which
predictors the lasso dropped, and which controls it kept.

## Task 2 — Ridge: shrink everything, select nothing

Change one argument to get the other classical penalty. L2 shrinks coefficients
towards zero in proportion to their size and never reaches it. Fit it on the
same grid and folds, and compare.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}

                       metrics = metric_set(roc_auc))
ridge_fit <- finalize_workflow(ridge_wf, select_best(ridge_res, metric = "roc_auc")) |>
  fit(data = train)
ridge_co  <- tidy(ridge_fit) |> arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
print(ridge_co, n = 13)

c(lasso_zeros = sum(lasso_co$estimate == 0),

check_selection(ridge_co, controls, label = "the CV-best ridge")
augment(ridge_fit, test) |>
```

## Worked example — the whole path, and what a clean model costs

A lasso does not fit one model. It fits a path: at every penalty, a different
set of survivors. Both libraries will hand you the whole thing, so there is no
reason to look at only the point the tuning chose.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
coef_path <- purrr::map_dfr(pen_grid$penalty, \(lam) tidy(lasso_fit, penalty = lam)) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(kind = if_else(term %in% controls, "control", "measured"))

ggplot(coef_path, aes(log10(penalty), estimate, group = term, colour = kind)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log10(best_pen$penalty), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(control = "firebrick", measured = "grey30")) +
  labs(x = "log10(penalty)", y = "standardised coefficient",
       colour = NULL, title = "Lasso path; dashed line is the CV-best penalty")

path <- coef_path |>
  summarise(kept_real     = sum(estimate != 0 & kind == "measured"),
            kept_controls = sum(estimate != 0 & kind == "control"),
            .by = penalty) |>
  left_join(collect_metrics(lasso_res) |> select(penalty, cv_auc = mean, std_err),
            by = "penalty")

path |> slice_min(penalty, n = 1, by = c(kept_real, kept_controls)) |> arrange(penalty)

# the largest penalty whose resampled AUC is still within one standard error
select_by_one_std_err(lasso_res, metric = "roc_auc", desc(penalty)) |> select(penalty)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rows, lines = [], []
for C, mean, sd in zip(Cs, lasso_search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"],
                       lasso_search.cv_results_["std_test_score"]):
    f = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", l1_ratio=1, C=C,
                                         max_iter=5000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    c = pd.Series(f[-1].coef_[0], index=X.columns)
    lines.append(c)
    rows.append({"C": round(C, 5),
                 "kept_real": int((c.drop(controls) != 0).sum()),
                 "kept_controls": int((c[controls] != 0).sum()),
                 "cv_auc": round(mean, 4), "std_err": round(sd / np.sqrt(10), 4)})

paths = pd.DataFrame(lines, index=Cs)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
for col in paths.columns:
    ax.plot(np.log10(paths.index), paths[col],
            color="firebrick" if col in controls else "grey")
ax.axvline(np.log10(lasso_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"]), ls="--", color="black")
ax.set_xlabel("log10(C)"); ax.set_ylabel("standardised coefficient")
ax.set_title("Lasso path; red is a control, dashed line is the CV-best C")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

path = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(path.drop_duplicates(subset=["kept_real", "kept_controls"], keep="last").to_string(index=False))

# the strongest penalty (smallest C) still within one standard error of the best
best = path["cv_auc"].idxmax()
within = path["cv_auc"] >= path.loc[best, "cv_auc"] - path.loc[best, "std_err"]
print("one-standard-error C:", path.loc[within, "C"].min())
```
:::

The table has one row for each distinct pair of survivor counts, printed at the
weakest penalty that achieves it. Three penalties on it are worth marking: the
one the tuning chose, the one at which the last control disappears, and the
strongest penalty whose resampled AUC is still within one standard error of the
best — the one-standard-error rule of @sec-decision-trees, which the cell above
prints. In R they are 0.0085, 0.0418 and 0.204, all different, and the
one-standard-error rule lands in the stretch of the path where `glucose` is the
only survivor. In Python they are `C` = 0.386, `C` = 0.0788 and `C` = 0.053,
and the last two keep the same five predictors. Neither language puts the
tuned penalty near either of the other two.

## Task 3 — Which of two correlated predictors survives

`age` and `pregnant` are correlated at about 0.74 in these 768 patients. A lasso given two
nearly interchangeable predictors does not split the coefficient between them;
it tends to keep one and zero the other. Which one it keeps is the question.

Refit at the penalty that clears the controls, on twenty bootstrap resamples of
the training rows, and tabulate which of the pair survives each time.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
clear_pen <- path |> filter(kept_controls == 0, kept_real > 0) |>
  slice_min(penalty, n = 1) |> pull(penalty)
clear_pen

pick_pair <- function(sp) {
  d  <- analysis(sp)
  wf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = d) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
    add_model(logistic_reg(penalty = clear_pen, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet"))
  co   <- tidy(fit(wf, data = d))
  kept <- intersect(c("______", "______"), co$term[co$estimate != 0])
  if (length(kept) == 0) "neither" else paste(kept, collapse = " + ")
}

set.seed(123)
boots <- bootstraps(train, times = ______, strata = diabetes)
table(vapply(boots$splits, pick_pair, character(1)))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The two string blanks are the correlated pair named in the paragraph above.
`bootstraps()` takes the number of resamples the paragraph asks for; twenty is
enough to see the instability and small enough to finish while you watch.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
clear_pen <- path |> filter(kept_controls == 0, kept_real > 0) |>
  slice_min(penalty, n = 1) |> pull(penalty)
clear_pen

pick_pair <- function(sp) {
  d  <- analysis(sp)
  wf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(recipe(diabetes ~ ., data = d) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
    add_model(logistic_reg(penalty = clear_pen, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet"))
  co   <- tidy(fit(wf, data = d))
  kept <- intersect(c("age", "pregnant"), co$term[co$estimate != 0])
  if (length(kept) == 0) "neither" else paste(kept, collapse = " + ")
}

set.seed(123)
boots <- bootstraps(train, times = 20, strata = diabetes)
table(vapply(boots$splits, pick_pair, character(1)))
```
:::
:::

```{python}
clear_C = path.loc[path["kept_controls"] == 0, "C"].max()
print(clear_C)

def pick_pair(seed):
    r   = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    idx = r.integers(0, len(X_tr), len(X_tr))
    f   = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                        LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", l1_ratio=1,
                                           C=clear_C, max_iter=5000)
                        ).fit(X_tr.iloc[idx], y_tr.iloc[idx])
    c    = pd.Series(f[-1].coef_[0], index=X.columns)
    kept = [v for v in ["______", "______"] if c[v] != 0]
    return " + ".join(kept) if kept else "neither"

print(pd.Series([pick_pair(100 + b) for b in range(______)]).value_counts())
```

## Worked answer
```{python}
clear_C = path.loc[path["kept_controls"] == 0, "C"].max()
print(clear_C)

def pick_pair(seed):
    r   = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    idx = r.integers(0, len(X_tr), len(X_tr))
    f   = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                        LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", l1_ratio=1,
                                           C=clear_C, max_iter=5000)
                        ).fit(X_tr.iloc[idx], y_tr.iloc[idx])
    c    = pd.Series(f[-1].coef_[0], index=X.columns)
    kept = [v for v in ["age", "pregnant"] if c[v] != 0]
    return " + ".join(kept) if kept else "neither"

print(pd.Series([pick_pair(100 + b) for b in range(20)]).value_counts())
```
:::
:::
:::

Nothing changed between those twenty fits except which patients were resampled.
Every one of them is a defensible analysis of these data, and they do not agree
on the variable list.

## The result that should bother you

The lasso did set coefficients to exactly zero, which is what it is for. Look
at which ones. In R it zeroed `insulin` and `triceps` — two measurements a
diabetes clinic takes — and kept all four random columns. In Python it zeroed
`insulin`, `triceps` and one of the four controls, and kept the other three.

Three steps.

1. The penalty was chosen to minimise cross-validated AUC and nothing else. At
   the chosen penalty — 0.0085 in R and `C` = 0.386 in Python, which is a
   penalty of 0.0048 in R's units — the resampled AUC is 0.777 with a standard error
   of 0.023, and 0.803 with a standard error of 0.015. A control column that
   happens to line up with the outcome in the training rows earns a small
   coefficient, and taking it away costs a little resampled AUC, so the tuning
   keeps it. Prediction was the objective. Selection was a side effect, and
   nobody asked the cross-validation to do it well.
2. The penalty that does clear the controls sits further along the path:
   0.0418 in R and `C` = 0.0788 in Python. It costs 0.007 and 0.006 of
   resampled AUC respectively, both comfortably inside one standard error, so
   the sparse model predicts just as well. But read the other column of the
   path table. Clearing the four worthless columns takes three real ones with
   it: the survivors fall from 7 to 4 in R and from 8 to 5 in Python.
3. And the list that comes out is not stable. At that same penalty, over twenty
   bootstrap resamples of the same 537 patients, R kept `age` alone 6 times,
   `pregnant` alone 7 times, both 5 times and neither twice; Python kept
   `pregnant` alone 12 times, `age` alone once, both 5 times and neither twice.
   The two are correlated at about 0.74, the penalty will pay for one of them,
   and which one it buys depends on which patients were resampled.

A lasso hands you a variable list with no uncertainty attached to it. The list
has at least as much sampling variability as any other estimate you have made
this week, and it hides it better, because a coefficient of exactly zero looks
like a decision rather than an estimate.

## What the penalty assumes

A penalty is not a neutral correction for small samples. It is a statement
about which coefficient values are plausible before the data arrives: an L2
penalty is exactly a normal prior on the coefficients centred at zero, and an
L1 penalty is a Laplace prior, which is peaked at zero and has no derivative
there — that kink is what produces exact zeros. Both say that a coefficient of 0.1 is more believable than one of
2, for every predictor equally.

Sometimes that is right. In a model with twelve standardised predictors and 537
patients, large coefficients usually are noise, and the test AUCs above say so.
But it is a claim about the biology, and it is being made by the fitting
procedure rather than by you. A penalty applied to a predictor you have strong
prior reason to believe in — a dose, an established risk factor — shrinks it
for the same reason it shrinks `noise4`, which is no reason at all. `glmnet`
lets you exempt a predictor with `penalty.factor`, and almost nobody does;
scikit-learn's `LogisticRegression` offers no equivalent at all.

## Reflection

1. Your collaborator reads the lasso output and says: "so insulin and triceps
   do not predict diabetes". Write the reply, in two sentences, without using
   the word "significant".
2. Task 3 produced a different variable list from each resample of the same
   537 patients. What would you have to report, instead of a variable list, for
   the reader to see that instability?
3. Regularisation and the random forest of @sec-random-forest are both answers
   to variance. Name one thing a penalised regression gives you that the forest
   cannot, and one thing the forest gives you that the penalty cannot.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) Something like: the lasso dropped them *given the other ten
predictors and this penalty*, which is a statement about redundancy at one
point on a path, not about their association with the outcome; refitting at a
smaller penalty keeps both. (2) Selection frequency across resamples — the
proportion of bootstraps in which each predictor survives, which is the idea
behind stability selection, and is Stretch 2. (3) The penalised regression
gives a coefficient with a sign and a magnitude a clinician can read, and a
model that extrapolates predictably; the forest captures interactions and
non-linearity nobody specified.

**Expected values.** Synthetic data; the two
languages split differently and both are given.

| | R, seed 123 (glmnet) | Python, random_state 123 (liblinear) |
|---|---|---|
| unpenalised test AUC | 0.842 | 0.774 |
| largest control coefficient, unpenalised | `noise4` 0.214, 4th of 12, p = 0.043 | `noise3` 0.128, 6th of 12 |
| CV-best penalty | 0.0085 | `C` = 0.386 |
| resampled AUC there | 0.777 ± 0.023 | 0.803 ± 0.015 |
| lasso coefficients set to zero | `triceps`, `insulin` | `triceps`, `insulin`, `noise` |
| lasso test AUC | 0.846 | 0.776 |
| ridge zeros / test AUC | 0 / 0.839 | 0 / 0.781 |
| penalty clearing all four controls | 0.0418, 4 real survivors | `C` = 0.0788, 5 real survivors |
| resampled AUC there | 0.770 ± 0.022 | 0.797 ± 0.014 |
| 20 bootstraps at that penalty | `age` 6, `pregnant` 7, both 5, neither 2 | `pregnant` 12, `age` 1, both 5, neither 2 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

The three test AUCs within a language — unpenalised, lasso, ridge — differ by
less than 0.01. Say that out loud: on 537 rows and twelve predictors the
penalty is not buying prediction. What it changes is the variable list, and
that is the thing the page is about.

**Common failures.** (1) Forgetting `step_normalize()` or `StandardScaler()`
and then reading the coefficient table: `insulin` and `glucose` are on scales
two orders of magnitude apart, the penalty hits them unequally, and the
selection is meaningless. (2) Reading `mixture` as the amount of penalty rather
than its type; the amount is `penalty`. (3) Expecting the `[fix]` from
`check_selection()` to go away — it is the result, and Task 1 is the one place
in the day where a check is supposed to fail. (4) In Python, `l1_ratio=1`
without `solver="liblinear"` or `"saga"`: lbfgs cannot do L1 and the error
message does not say so clearly.

**Timing.** The page runs end to end in about twenty seconds in each
language, tuning and bootstraps included. Task 3 is
the one to protect; if the room is behind, run the path worked example as a
demonstration and give them `clear_pen` directly.
:::
:::

Elastic net is `mixture` strictly between 0 and 1 (`l1_ratio` in Python). Tune
over a two-dimensional grid of `penalty` and `mixture`, and see whether
anything beats both endpoints by more than its standard error. Then say what
the elastic net does with `age` and `pregnant` that the lasso would not.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Report a frequency, not a list
Extend Task 3: across 100 bootstrap resamples, record every predictor's
selection frequency rather than only the correlated pair's. Sort them. That
table is what a lasso can honestly support, and the controls give you the
reference level for "selected by chance".
:::

## Stretch 3 — Two rankings of the same data
@sec-importance ranks the same twelve columns by permutation importance on a
random forest. Put that ranking next to the order in which the lasso path drops
the columns. Where they disagree, which would you trust, and what would settle
it?
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can fit a penalised logistic regression with the penalty
chosen by cross-validation in either language, read off which coefficients it
set to exactly zero, and state the AUC cost of the sparser model.

**Cannot:** that the variables the lasso kept are the variables that matter.
The selection moved when the rows were resampled and the controls survived the
penalty the cross-validation chose, so the variable list is an output of the
procedure as much as of the biology. Nor can you claim the penalty is
assumption-free: it encodes a preference for small coefficients that you did
not derive from anything clinical. @sec-day6 asks what the model did, variable
by variable and patient by patient, which is a different question and has its
own controls.
